newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu returns home to face Jerusalem dispute.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu returns home to face Jerusalem dispute.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu returned on Monday from a U.S. visit to face political trouble at home over the issue of building a new Jewish neighbourhood in Arab East Jerusalem.

Israel's Jerusalem mayor Ehud Olmert said he would send bulldozers to the Har Homa site within days to pave the way for construction if Israeli media reports proved true that Netanyahu had frozen plans to build 6,500 housing units.

Israel's Peace Now movement -- an opponent of Jewish settlement on land captured from the Arabs in the 1967 Middle East war -- said building on Har Homa, a hill of pine forests near the Arab village Sur Bahir, would ignite Arab violence.

"Har Homa would be another Jerusalem tunnel," Peace Now spokesman Mossi Raz said, referring to Israeli-Palestinian clashes last September following Israel's opening of a new entrance to a tourist tunnel near Moslem holy sites in the city.
The violence, which threatened to wreck the Israel-PLO peace process, claimed the lives of 61 Palestinians and 15 Israelis.
Netanyahu could face a revolt in his own Likud party and from rightist coalition partners if he kills the project.
"I see this issue of Har Homa as a watershed," Olmert said.

"This government exists on the basis of a parliamentary majority and I find it difficult to believe there will be a majority for a policy that does not fulfil detailed commitments on Jerusalem," he told Israel Radio.

Foreign Minister David Levy rallied to Netanyahu's side, calling on right-wing politicians to hold their fire until the prime minister could clarify the issue. The Har Homa project's supporters say it will cement Israel's disputed claim to all of Jerusalem.
"There is no decision not to build in Jerusalem," Levy told the radio.
Netanyahu made no comments to the press immediately after returning from a four-day visit to the United States.

Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai said on Sunday that a ministerial committee on Jerusalem, chaired by Netanyahu, would decide whether to go ahead with plans announced by the previous Labour-led government to build the Har Homa project.
Israel Radio said the committee would meet on Tuesday.

Binyamin Begin, a hardline member of the Likud who quit the cabinet over the government's handover of most of the West Bank town of Hebron to the PLO last month, accused the Israeli leader of "dividing Jerusalem".
Netanyahu used the phrase as his rallying cry in defeating Labour Prime Minister Shimon Peres in last year's national election.

The Har Homa controversy dominated news reports in Israel on Monday and overshadowed Sunday's mainly ceremonial resumption of Israeli-PLO talks on implementing interim agreements signed since a landmark peace deal in 1993.
Israeli and Palestinian teams were to meet for detailed discussions on Monday.

The agenda for the interim talks includes arrangements for Palestinian sea and air ports, a "safe passage" between the West Bank and Gaza, economic, civil and financial affairs and "people to people" grass-roots cooperation projects, officials said.
Palestinians warned Netanyahu to resist the appeals of Israeli rightists to speed Jewish settlement construction.
"The Israeli government should not pre-empt these (final status) negotiations by trying to put fait accompli policies on the ground," Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat said on Sunday.
"All these activities, whether confiscation of land, settlements, Judaisation of Jerusalem, must cease, must stop immediately," Erekat told Reuters.
